segments.text: I thank you heartily for your kind letter of
Decr 28th &
segments.label: org

segments.text: for all the information in your power on the resistance of plants to your climate, & on their acclimatisation on your different elevations.
I am especially obliged for your remarks on the several species having
alpine & lowland
segments.label: org

segments.text: forms, & for what you mention about some having & some not having intermediate varieties.— I will quote this part of your note; for it was exactly a point on which I wanted information.
You state that the latter ie lowland forms have much smaller flowers, & frequently more numerous; leaves, longer,
narrower &
segments.label: org

segments.text: less coriaceous. I copy this for there is often a mistake in “latters” & “formers”— If I do not hear to contrary, I will assume that this description does apply to the low-land forms.— I see you do not mention “
hariness”,—a
segments.label: place

segments.text: character usually given to alpine forms, but which
Hooker
segments.label: org

segments.text: has been looking into for me & disputes or rather overthrows.
I was lately struck by a remark in
U. States
segments.label: place

segments.text: naturalist, namely that introduced or naturalised plants at first overrun the whole country, & then in some degree diminish in numbers. Do you know of anything like this in
Ceylon
segments.label: place

segments.text: , where you have so many naturalised plants?— I can see some likely causes of error in the foregoing remark, & yet the fact in itself seems probable.
How interesting it would be to cultivate some of the upland forms in the low country & trace probable changes in successive generations.—
With my very sincere thanks, Yours very truly |
Ch
segments.label: person

segments.text: Darwin
segments.label: person
